newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Opposition plans fresh protest in Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: Opposition plans fresh protest in Kabila's Congo.

text.p: Opposition militants in Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo announced plans to defy a government ban once again by holding a march on Friday to back demands for early elections or a role in government.
"We want a transition lasting one year until elections, and if it is going to be longer then we want to take part in government," opposition firebrand Joseph Olenghankoy told Reuters on Thursday.

Olenghankoy, an ally of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, confirmed that the march would take place. Soldiers broke up early marches by firing in the air. They followed the most recent march closely but did not intervene.

Kabila won approval from much of the international community for a pledge to hold elections by April 1999 in the vast state where infrastructures collapsed during dictator Mobutu Sese Seko's three decades of rule.

"If they refuse (our demands), that will create a climate of frustration and we may be obliged to take up arms; it seems it is the only language the international community understands," Olenghankoy said.
United States embassy officials said U.S. envoy Bill Richardson was expected to arrive in the capital Kinshasa on Friday for talks.

Officials said that Kabila, who returned to the southern mining city of Lubumbashi instead of Kinshasa after his first foreign trip as head of state, would hold his weekly cabinet meeting in Lubumbashi on Friday.

"The president plans to hold the weekly cabinet meeting tomorrow in Lubumbashi instead of in Kinshasa," said one senior official after Kabila returned from the Organisation of African Unity summit in the Zimbabwe. He did not say why.

Government officials said Kabila met businessmen in Lubumbashi on Wednesday and they discussed strengthening the trade route which links southern Africa with the copper and cobalt rich Katanga province in southern Congo, the president's home region, and the central diamond-producing Kasai region.

Since ousting Mobutu in May after a seven-month bush war, Kabila has made only one major public appearance in the chaotic riverside capital of five million people -- at his swearing-in ceremony, where he was heckled.
Demonstrations against Kabila's exclusion of Tshisekedi from his government and the presence of Rwandan ethnic Tutsi troops among his army erupted shortly after he arrived in the capital.
Tshisekedi says the post of prime minister -- a post dropped by Kabila -- is constitutionally his.

Mobutu, who dominated Africa's third largest nation for over three decades, was unpopular in Kinshasa and chose to spend little time there in the last years of his reign. He preferred to remain at his northern jungle palace of Gbadolite.
